label: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question (original, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Pinefield Furniture sells £80,000 of office desks to customers on 60-day credit. The sales are recognised in its income statement, but its suppliers must be paid this week.
question.stem: Which conclusion best explains why reporting a profit from the sale does not guarantee Pinefield can pay its suppliers this week?

options.label: A
options.text: The credit sale has already increased the bank balance by £80,000.

options.label: B
options.text: Revenue can be recorded before customers pay, so the firm may be profitable while short of cash.

options.label: C
options.text: A business cannot report a profit unless all customers have paid in full.

options.label: D
options.text: Profit and net cash flow always have the same value over any given month.

option_rationale: A is incorrect because recognised credit sales do not necessarily bring immediate cash receipts.
B is correct because sales revenue may be recognised before cash is collected, creating a short-term liquidity problem.
C is incorrect because accounting performance can recognise revenue before cash collection.
D is incorrect because accounting profit differs from cash flow because of timing, accruals and non-cash costs.
mark_scheme.model_answer: B. Credit sales can affect reported profit before the cash arrives; the firm must forecast and finance the period until customers settle invoices.
